title: Lifting CSP sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
formal: For every finite family \(\Pi\) of Boolean predicates of a fixed arity, does the following implication hold? If no \(o(\sqrt n)\)-bit sketching algorithm nontrivially approximates Max-CSP(\(\Pi\)), then no \(o(n)\)-bit single-pass streaming algorithm nontrivially approximates it. Nontrivial approximation, sketching and the polynomial stream-length convention are defined below.
why: A universal implication would upgrade a broad sketching classification to a fundamental limitation on all small-memory streaming algorithms. A counterexample would show that some CSPs admit an informative sequential summary even though every substantially smaller mergeable summary is approximation resistant.
status_note: The 2025 source states this as a conjecture. A substantial April 2026 theorem now gives LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, but the checked text does not explicitly establish or refute Conjecture 8 for every sketching-resistant family. Status remains uncertain rather than certifying that the 2025 question survives that theorem. The card’s mathematical statement is complete, and its polynomial-length convention is identified explicitly.

progress.text: Chou, Golovnev, Sudan and Velusamy publish the finite-CSP sketching dichotomy.
Singer poses the lifting implication as Conjecture 8 and explicitly allows that counterexamples may exist.
Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy establish LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, creating a stronger framework that must be compared with the conjecture’s premise.

importance.reason: A broad proposed transfer of approximation resistance across both models and space thresholds, with implications for the classification of streaming CSPs.

sentences: Each fixed predicate family defines a maximum constraint-satisfaction problem.
A nontrivial approximation beats the best constant lower bound on the optimum by a fixed amount.
The conjecture lifts resistance to small mergeable sketches into resistance to all sublinear-space streaming algorithms.
Both the algorithm model and the space threshold change in the implication.
The 2026 LP-gap lower bounds are recorded without claiming a verified resolution of this exact lifting statement.

definitions: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\) and a nonempty finite family \(\Pi\subseteq\{\pi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\}\). A constraint on \(n\geq k\) variables consists of a predicate \(\pi\in\Pi\) and an ordered tuple of \(k\) distinct indices in \([n]\). An instance \(\Phi\) is a nonempty list of such constraints; repetitions are allowed and every occurrence has unit weight. For an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), its value is the fraction of constraint occurrences it satisfies, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) is the maximum over assignments. Let \(\rho(\Pi)=\inf_{n\geq k,\Phi}\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\). Padding with unused variables makes this the limiting trivial approximation threshold. A nontrivial approximation has a fixed \(\delta>0\), with \(\rho(\Pi)+\delta\leq1\), and outputs a value \(v\) satisfying \((\rho(\Pi)+\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\leq v\leq\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance and order. The algorithm need not output an assignment. A deterministic streaming algorithm has a finite state represented by \(s\) bits, a fixed initial state, an update map taking the current state and next constraint, and a final output map. It reads the constraint list once in an adversarial order. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic algorithms, chosen independently of the list. Local computation and the choice of this distribution are unrestricted; this is the nonuniform randomness model used for the source’s lower bounds. A sketching algorithm additionally has a state map \(K\) on lists and a binary combination map \(H\), with \(K(\sigma\tau)=H(K(\sigma),K(\tau))\) for every pair of lists whose concatenation is allowed; its updates append a singleton through this map, and its output depends only on the sketch. Randomized sketches are distributions over such deterministic schemes. Commutativity and linearity of the sketches are not separately required. Editorial length convention: an algorithmic space regime must handle every fixed polynomial length bound. Precisely, to admit nontrivial approximation in \(o(b(n))\) space means that there is one fixed \(\delta>0\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), there is an algorithm family for all lists of length at most \(n^d\), with worst-case state size \(s_d(n)\) satisfying \(s_d(n)/b(n)\to0\). The algorithm may depend on \(\Pi,d,\delta,n\), but not on the input list; the ratio improvement \(\delta\) does not depend on \(n\) or \(d\). The two occurrences of “no” in the conjecture negate this full definition.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every predicate family in the stated model, or give a fixed family that is resistant to nontrivial o(√n)-space sketching and a nontrivial o(n)-space streaming approximation for that family. Both parts of a counterexample need proofs. A faster approximation for a family already admitting nontrivial small sketches, or a lower bound under an additional condition not proved for all families in the premise, is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: This is Conjecture 8 of Singer’s column. It simultaneously enlarges the algorithm class and the permitted memory, while asking only whether any fixed improvement over the trivial ratio is possible. It does not claim that every approximation threshold of every CSP stays unchanged as space increases.

The sketching dichotomy gives polylogarithmic-space algorithms or square-root-space lower bounds, with a small slack in the approximation thresholds. Its definition of a sketch permits general mergeable summaries; restricting the premise to linear sketches would be a different statement.

Max-DiCut illustrates why the premise matters. Its trivial ratio is one quarter, while small sketches already give a ratio approaching four ninths. Better streaming approximations using more memory therefore do not by themselves refute the resistance implication in this card.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy’s April 2026 manuscript proves linear-space lower bounds from integrality gaps of the basic linear programming relaxation. That relaxation assigns a distribution of local assignments to each constraint and requires consistent one-variable marginals on shared variables. Its ratio is not defined by the sketching premise in this card.

The same manuscript gives a tight classification for bounded-degree instances and explicitly continues to distinguish general sketching lower bounds from streaming lower bounds. Applying its theorem to Conjecture 8 requires a theorem connecting every resistant predicate family to the needed LP gap. This review does not claim that such a connection has been proved or disproved.
